meta.titre: Marriage in African Traditional Religion at Advanced Level: a union of families and the continuity of life
meta.sous_theme: Purpose, stages and social meaning of marriage in ATR, and its link with children
tags: A Level Religious Studies - atr marriage and family

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Religious Studies past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In many Cameroonian communities a marriage is arranged and celebrated by two families rather than by two people alone. Elders speak for each side, gifts are exchanged, relatives travel from far away and the whole village shares the joy. A couple without children is often a cause of worry for everyone. This is why Religious Studies examiners return to marriage and family in African Traditional Religion (ATR) and ask you to examine, explain or justify its importance.

items: African Traditional Religion (ATR) is the name given to the indigenous beliefs and practices of African peoples, handed down by custom, oral tradition and ritual rather than by a written scripture or a single founder.
Many African peoples believe in a Supreme Being, in spirits and in ancestors who remain part of the family after death.
In most traditional African societies the extended family, lineage or clan is the basic social unit, not the individual alone.

sections.titre: Marriage and family in ATR: why marriage matters and why it is tied to children
sections.contenu_markdown:
### A word of caution
ATR is not one uniform religion: customs differ from one people to another. In your answer write 'in many African societies' or 'among many peoples', and avoid claiming that every community does exactly the same thing.

### What marriage means
In many African societies marriage is seen as a duty and as a normal stage of the life cycle, together with birth, initiation and death. Through marriage a person becomes a full adult member of the community. Remaining unmarried is often regarded as incomplete or unusual.

### Why marriage is important
| Aspect | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Religious | Marriage is understood as willed by the Supreme Being and as a matter in which the ancestors are interested. In many places prayers or libations to God or the ancestors accompany the rites, so that the union may be blessed. |
| Social | It joins two families or lineages, creating bonds of friendship, alliance and mutual help. Elders from both sides take part in the negotiations and act as witnesses. |
| Procreation | Children continue the family line and the family name. They are seen as a gift of God and a blessing, and they make sure the ancestors are remembered by descendants. |
| Economic | Husband and wife share the work of the household, the farm and the market, and children later support their parents in old age. |
| Moral | Sexual relations belong within marriage, and faithfulness is expected. Elders advise the couple and settle quarrels. |

### Marriage as a process
In many societies marriage is not a single event but a series of stages: choice or introduction, enquiries by the families, negotiations, the handing over of the marriage payment (often called bridewealth) and a celebration. The payment is usually explained as a sign of gratitude to the bride's family and a seal of the agreement between the two families. It is not meant to buy a person.

### Marriage and procreation
In many peoples the birth of children is the main fruit of marriage. A childless marriage is a deep sorrow for the couple and for both families, because the line may end. People often turn to diviners, sacrifices or other remedies, and in some societies a further wife may be taken. In some peoples a newborn child is believed to be an ancestor who has returned, so birth links the living, the dead and the unborn.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command word asks you to look closely at a topic and weigh it, not just list it.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Choose four or five reasons (religious, social, procreation, economic, moral). Give each its own paragraph with the pattern point, explanation, example. Finish with a short judgement on which reason is the weightiest and why.

variantes.nom: 'Justify' a claim such as 'marriage and procreation belong together'
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you are given a statement and must defend it with reasons.
variantes.contenu_markdown: State that you will defend the claim. Give three or four reasons: children continue the lineage, children are a blessing from God, ancestors need descendants, a childless marriage is a misfortune. End by acknowledging briefly that peoples differ and that companionship and cooperation are also valued, so the claim is strong without being the only truth.

sections.enonce_markdown: Assess the part played by the extended family in the making and keeping of a marriage in African Traditional Religion. (25 marks)

etapes.action: Analyse the command word and the key terms.
etapes.justification: 'Assess' asks for explanation and a judgement. 'Making' and 'keeping' show that the answer must cover two stages: before the wedding and after it.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Two parts: the family in making the marriage, the family in keeping it, then a judgement.

etapes.action: Build a plan with a short introduction and a conclusion.
etapes.justification: A plan keeps the answer balanced and avoids telling a story of a wedding.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Introduction (say that practice varies), family in making, family in keeping, judgement.

etapes.action: Develop the making of the marriage with evidence.
etapes.justification: Each point needs a fact and an explanation of its meaning.
etapes.resultat_markdown: In many societies elders, not only the couple, approve the choice, make enquiries about the other family and lead the negotiations. The marriage payment is handed over between families, and the ancestors are addressed in prayer, showing that the union concerns the whole lineage.

etapes.action: Develop the keeping of the marriage with evidence.
etapes.justification: A second paragraph on the life of the couple shows depth.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Elders advise the couple, settle quarrels and support them in hardship. Relatives share the care of children, so the marriage rests on a wide network of help.

etapes.justification: A judgement turns a description into an assessment.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The family's role is very large in ATR because marriage joins lineages, but today the free choice of the couple and the pressures of town life reduce it in some places.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer, in brief. In many African societies marriage is not a private contract but a union of two families. In the making of the marriage, elders approve the choice, hold the negotiations, receive the marriage payment as a seal of the agreement and call upon the ancestors to bless the couple. In the keeping of the marriage, relatives advise, settle disputes, help in difficulty and share in raising the children. For these reasons the extended family has a central part in ATR marriage. Practice varies among peoples and, in modern towns, the couple's own choice counts for more, but the principle that marriage concerns the whole community remains strong.

items.erreur_markdown: 'In ATR, a man pays bridewealth, so he buys his wife.'
items.pourquoi_faux: This misunderstands the purpose of the payment. In many societies it expresses gratitude to the bride's family, seals the agreement between two families and gives the marriage public recognition.
items.correction_markdown: 'The marriage payment is a sign of appreciation and a seal of the bond between the two families. It is not the purchase of a person.'

items.erreur_markdown: 'All Africans marry in exactly the same way: the bride's family always does X.'
items.pourquoi_faux: ATR is made up of many peoples with different customs. An over-generalisation is a factual error and loses marks.
items.correction_markdown: 'Among many peoples ...' or 'In many African societies ...', followed by features that are widely shared.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing the whole wedding day in story form when the question asks about the importance of marriage.
items.pourquoi_faux: A narrative does not answer an 'examine' or 'assess' question: the examiner wants reasons.
items.correction_markdown: Turn each stage into a reason: why the family is involved, what the ancestors' blessing means, how the ceremony joins two lineages.

items.erreur_markdown: Quoting church or mosque marriage vows as part of ATR practice.
items.pourquoi_faux: Mixing traditions is a content error. ATR rites rest on custom and on belief in God, spirits and ancestors.
items.correction_markdown: Use only ATR features: the role of elders, the marriage payment, rites addressed to God or the ancestors, the link with the lineage.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that children are the only reason for marriage in ATR.
items.pourquoi_faux: Procreation is central, but companionship, cooperation, economic support and moral order also matter.
items.correction_markdown: 'Procreation is the main fruit of marriage in many societies, but marriage also brings social, economic and moral benefits.'

items.enonce_markdown: State four reasons why many African societies regard marriage as a duty rather than a free choice.
items.solution_markdown: Award a mark for each valid point, up to four: (1) it is a normal stage of the life cycle and a sign of full adulthood; (2) it continues the family line through children; (3) it is believed to be willed by God and watched over by the ancestors; (4) it unites two families in friendship and mutual help; (5) it provides help in work and care in old age. **Any four of these points, each stated clearly, earn full marks.**

items.enonce_markdown: Explain why a childless marriage is seen as a serious misfortune in many ATR communities.
items.solution_markdown: Model points. (1) Children continue the lineage and the family name, so a marriage without them threatens the end of the line. (2) Descendants remember the ancestors by libations and prayers, so childlessness is also a religious problem. (3) Children are viewed as a blessing from God, so their absence raises worry about the couple's relation to God or the ancestors. (4) Children share in work and support their parents in old age. (5) The families of both partners are affected, so the sorrow is social as well as personal. **Four developed points, with a brief reference to the variety among peoples, earn full marks.**

items.enonce_markdown: 'In ATR the wedding of two persons is really the wedding of two families.' To what extent is this statement true?
items.solution_markdown: Plan. Agree with the statement to a large extent: elders choose or approve, negotiate and witness; the marriage payment passes between families; rites involve the ancestors of both lineages; children belong to the wider family; relatives help to keep the marriage stable. Then qualify: the couple's personal feelings, consent and companionship matter and are more important today, and customs differ among peoples. **Conclusion: the statement is largely true because ATR sees the individual as part of a community, although modern life gives the couple more voice.**

items_markdown: ATR customs vary from people to people, so write 'in many African societies' and avoid claims about all Africans.
Marriage is a duty and a stage of the life cycle that makes a person a full member of the community.
Marriage joins two families or lineages: elders negotiate, witness and advise, and the marriage payment seals the bond.
Procreation is the main fruit of marriage because children continue the lineage, are a blessing from God and keep the ancestors remembered.
For 'examine', 'assess' and 'justify', give reasons with explanation and a short judgement, never a story of a wedding.
